reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A rare but serious secondary angle closure caused by misdirection of aqueous into or behind the vitreous, pushing the whole lens-iris diaphragm forward
It classically arises after intraocular surgery, especially incisional glaucoma or cataract surgery in eyes with angle closure, but can follow laser procedures or occur spontaneously
The hallmark is a uniformly shallow or flat anterior chamber, both centrally and peripherally, in combination with raised or normal pressure and a patent iridotomy
The patent iridotomy and shallow central chamber distinguish it from pupillary-block angle closure, which the iridotomy would relieve
It must be differentiated from suprachoroidal haemorrhage and choroidal effusion, which can also flatten the chamber after surgery
Initial treatment is intensive cycloplegia to tighten the zonule and pull the lens back, together with pressure-lowering and anti-inflammatory therapy, and aqueous suppressants
Laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid, sometimes with the posterior capsule, can re-establish forward aqueous flow, and refractory cases require vitrectomy to relieve the block
Miotics tend to worsen the condition and should be avoided, whereas cycloplegics help
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant glaucoma, or aqueous misdirection, is thought to result from an abnormal anteriorly displaced relationship between the ciliary processes, lens equator, and anterior vitreous face, which diverts aqueous posteriorly into or behind the vitreous body instead of forward into the anterior chamber. Trapped aqueous raises pressure in the vitreous compartment and pushes the lens-iris diaphragm forward, producing uniform shallowing or flattening of the entire anterior chamber and secondary angle closure. A ciliary-block or hyaloid element impedes normal forward aqueous movement. Because the mechanism is behind the iris, a patent peripheral iridotomy does not relieve it, and interventions that draw the diaphragm backward or open the hyaloid pathway are needed to break the cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Pupillary-block angle closure (relieved by patent iridotomy)
Overfiltration with a flat bleb after trabeculectomy
Pupillary block from a swollen or dislocated lens
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp assessment showing uniform central and peripheral chamber shallowing
Confirmation of a patent peripheral iridotomy
B-scan ultrasonography to exclude suprachoroidal haemorrhage and choroidal effusion
Ultrasound biomicroscopy or anterior segment OCT to assess the ciliary body and anterior chamber configuration
Gonioscopy to document the closed angle
redFlags: A uniformly shallow or flat chamber after intraocular surgery despite a patent iridotomy
Rising pressure with progressive chamber flattening requiring urgent intervention
Failure to distinguish it from a suprachoroidal haemorrhage, which needs very different management
Worsening after miotic treatment given in the mistaken belief it is pupillary block
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition many eyes respond to cycloplegic and medical therapy or to laser hyaloidotomy, but the condition can be difficult to control and may need vitrectomy; delayed or misdirected treatment risks persistent flat chamber, corneal decompensation, and glaucomatous visual loss.
pitfalls: Treating it as pupillary block and giving miotics, which aggravate the misdirection
Missing a suprachoroidal haemorrhage or choroidal effusion as the cause of the flat chamber
Repeating an iridotomy when one is already patent instead of addressing the hyaloid block
Delaying vitrectomy in medically unresponsive cases
Failing to treat the fellow eye's angle-closure risk that predisposed to the original condition
management: Intensive topical cycloplegia with an agent such as atropine to tighten the zonule and draw the lens-iris diaphragm posteriorly
Aqueous suppressants including beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, with hyperosmotic agents to reduce vitreous volume and lower intraocular pressure
Topical corticosteroid to reduce inflammation, and cessation of any miotics, which aggravate the condition
Nd:YAG laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid face, with capsulotomy in pseudophakic eyes, to re-establish forward aqueous flow when medical therapy fails
Pars plana vitrectomy, often combined with irido-zonulo-hyaloidectomy or lens extraction, for refractory cases
Exclude and manage mimics such as suprachoroidal haemorrhage and choroidal effusion before escalating surgery
Prophylactic cycloplegia and avoidance of miotics in the fellow eye, with prompt vitreoretinal referral
